(Steal / discuss / argue – all welcome)

I defined the ICPs and their behavior patterns. For example: marketers / founders who are building a strat right now will visit 5+ insight cards per session.

Metrics only become meaningful after enough unique sessions. In most cases, 2–3K unique visitors is enough for accurate conversion and retention math.

5. Next: growth paths
Since there are multiple ICPs with different behavior patterns, the MVP should reveal which category has the best ICP fit – so we can scale in that direction. That’s why I already have several growth scenarios, each with $$ projections, risks, and a signal map.

6. Pre-release backlog
Based on everything above, I know what actions I need to track to make the next decisions – so I already have additional CTAs and survey blocks in my backlog, ready for the dev team to pick up.

I just spent the last four days in Iraq.

I am shocked at how easy it is for the media to sell a picture when reality couldn’t be more different.

Even in war, life moves on. The people are Iraq are warm, kind, and considerate. Not once was danger felt, although there certainly were nerves in the group. 

In a total shock — I actually met a Zionist Iraqi, who had a Star of David tattooed on his neck. Was not expecting to see that at all. 

While I was there, I continued by tradition of wrapping tefillin. I may have been the only person that day in Iraq to perform that Mitzvah and it felt especially meaningful in light of the large Jewish community that Iraq used to have.

I’ve come away with many stories, probably will make a video of it soon. 

But a main takeaway: there is tremendous opportunity for those willing to take risks in life. If you just show a little willingness to ignore the lies you’re fed, a whole world opens up to you.

⚒️ DAILY METALS PULSE — WEEKEND EDITION
Sunday, 18 October 2026

Floating reactors buying uranium. Old mine stockpiles delivering fresh value. China accelerating gold purchases.

Four developments worth a closer look:

☢️ URANIUM — A new customer is securing fuel

Bluecore Energy announced the purchase of low-enriched uranium this week for its floating nuclear development programme, following a $50 million seed financing.

The material still needs fuel fabrication, and deployment remains ahead. But this is an actual uranium purchase from a developer moving toward testing.

What interests me: maritime nuclear is beginning to translate engineering ambitions into fuel procurement. Another potential source of future demand to follow.

🥈 SILVER — The interesting detail inside Aya’s record quarter

$AYA reported record quarterly production of 2.03 million silver-equivalent ounces, up 51% year over year.

Roughly 26% came from reclaiming historical pyrite stockpiles at Boumadine. Meanwhile, Zgounder itself delivered record silver production of approximately 1.50 million ounces.

There is value in material already sitting above ground. The distinction matters, though: that stockpile contribution has a limited life. Sustained growth still requires sustained mine performance.

🔌 COPPER — A strike ends; the bigger challenge remains

Sunday’s fresh development: workers ratified an agreement ending the Centinela strike in Chile. Antofagasta said production had remained normal, so the immediate change is reduced disruption risk.

The longer-term warning came from Teck’s CEO on Thursday: he sees a potential 2035 supply shortfall equivalent to around 30 tier-one mines.

That is his forecast, but it illustrates the scale of investment copper may require.

🥇 GOLD — China’s buying accelerated during a pullback

Thursday’s World Gold Council update showed China added 23 tonnes to official gold reserves in September, its largest monthly purchase since October 2023.

That brought Q3 purchases to 63 tonnes. Chinese gold ETF holdings also reached a month-end record of 304 tonnes.

Official buying and investment demand strengthened even as prices retreated. Jewellery demand remains weaker, making the identity of the buyer particularly interesting.

👀 NEXT WEEK

I’m watching copper’s reaction to the Chile settlement, the direction of US bond yields, and miners’ production updates. Fuel procurement, durable output and reserve accumulation remain central to my metals thesis.

when I started in crypto in 2017, I had no idea what I was doing.

I threw a few hundred bucks at some random ICOs and somehow turned it into like $30k within half a year. then obviously lost it all when the bubble burst in 2018.

but I was euphoric and completely hooked. and the conclusion I walked away with was as left curve as it was brilliant:

altcoins gud.

so I did the only logical thing. I took out a loan at the end of 2018 and went all in. hit a few small runners in 2019, and founded Moonrock Capital.

decent capital to play with, a brand to invest under, and a strong left curve thesis. I was perfectly positioned for what came next:

the biggest bull run in crypto history. I turned a mid 5-figure personal portfolio into a mid 8-figure one for Moonrock.

but here's the interesting part:

the exact left curve approach that made me didn't evolve with me. I slowly turned into a textbook mid curvoor.

it started with NFTs I never fully understood and hence just lost money on them. then when memecoin mania exploded, I refused to touch it and just hated from the sidelines. after living through FTX, Luna and every other blow up, the PTSD made it almost impossible to believe in anything again, especially something that looked that stupid.

I don't regret it, and in hindsight I was mostly right. but I still left a lot of money on the table. what it did give me was time to think. about what comes next, and what kind of investor I actually want to be.

because here's what I realized: all the catalysts we kept waiting for, the pro-crypto president, the ETFs, the institutional flows, none of them moved the needle the way everyone promised.

and the reason is simple. the days of trading purely on narratives and speculation are over. it was fun while it lasted, but valuations got too outrageous to be justified by vibes alone. at some point you actually have to step up and deliver.

the casino will always exist in some form. but I'm convinced it keeps shrinking until it's just a small side niche. and that's completely fine.

look at Hyperliquid, PumpFun, Collector Crypt, the entire DeFi ecosystem over the last 1-2 years. the pattern is impossible to miss:

projects that create real value, that people genuinely want to use and pay for, massively outperform the ones that don't.

groundbreaking, I know.

we are finally maturing as an industry. the experimental decade was fun and brought incredible innovation. but the next decade is about noticing which experiments actually worked, and backing them with everything.

left curve made me. mid curve humbled me. who knows whether I am on the right side of the curve now, but I've never been more convinced about what's coming:

the longest and most rewarding cycle crypto has ever seen.

the Golden Age of Onchain Businesses.

Jeff drank a bit too much of his own Kool-Aid in this recent Odd Lots clip. I think it's important to clear up a distinction that makes all the difference.

Democratizing access to wealth creation is NOT the same as democratizing access to speculation.

Many of us genuinely want broader participation in attractive investment opportunities. The growing wealth inequality produced by the current system is tearing at the seams of society, something I've spoken about many times.

But let's be clear: listing pre-IPO perpetual futures does absolutely nothing to democratize the wealth being created in private markets.

I've seen this misleading narrative pushed repeatedly by perp DEXs lately, and it needs to be called out.

A pre-IPO perp creates ZERO underlying wealth. It's a zero-sum contract before costs, and negative-sum after them. No capital flows to the company. No ownership changes hands. No new economic opportunity is created.

Every long has a short. There is no free lunch in simply going long something before its IPO, and funding costs can even determine the outcome more than any price moves. TRADING access is NOT INVESTING access.

In fact, in many ways pre-IPO perps are almost the antithesis of democratized access:

They create the illusion of participation in private-market wealth creation, while actually offering retail a speculative instrument whose mechanics they are often poorly equipped to understand.

The result is a playground for the FEW sophisticated traders who understand funding, oracle design, and liquidation mechanics to extract value from the MANY who don't.

To give credit where it's due, Robinhood's efforts toward sourcing actual employee shares, placing them into SPVs, and tokenizing genuine spot ownership are much closer to meaningful democratization.

That can unlock real economic value by allowing employees to exchange some of their expected upside for liquidity, while giving new investors actual economic exposure. A legitimate financial trade-off, without the funding-rate and liquidation shenanigans.

I'm strongly aligned with expanding access to investment opportunities. And I believe advances in AI and blockchain can dramatically lower the barriers to discovering, structuring, and distributing them.

But let's not BS ourselves that launching another zero-sum casino contract is moving the needle on wealth inequality.

What would actually move the needle is bringing real capital formation and ownership onchain. Giving investors access to productive, illiquid assets like data centers, GPUs, and select startup investing, where capital can actually finance growth and share in the resulting value creation.

These opportunities are harder to structure, underwrite, and bring to market, and we haven't seen many compelling implementations onchain yet. 

Hopefully this will change soon and, as the industry matures, we can direct more of our energy toward actually expanding access to wealth creation.

Clip below. Was glad to see @tracyalloway push back on this framing, and to Jeff's credit, after this he does seem to walk back his original position somewhat.

Hello, friends,

There’s nothing like a Sunday for discussing current market conditions. And that’s exactly what we’re going to do today.

When we encounter a difficult situation, we like to categorize it.

For example, is this a problem that money can solve? Or, more relevant to the current situation, can we learn something from it and draw useful lessons?

That is what we’ll explore here.

The world’s leading pharmaceutical and biotech analyst is Umer Raffat, who works in New York for Evercore ISI.

As we do every weekend, we listened to his weekly podcast. This time, he opened with the topic of fund performance.

Here are a few things we learned.

First, the chaos in fund performance is not limited to biotech. According to ISI, technology funds are also going through a difficult and chaotic period.

This suggests that the current situation may also be connected to rising interest rates, in addition to the performance of $MRNA, a subject we have discussed extensively before.

Within biotech, ISI reports that market-neutral funds are down approximately 2% this year, while long-biased funds are down by double digits, except for a few fortunate funds that held stocks involved in M&A transactions.

Just how chaotic is the situation?

We have already seen junk stocks, led by $MRNA, skyrocket.

At the same time, large pharmaceutical stocks have rallied strongly, benefiting from a flight to safety.

The DRG index has gained approximately 15% over the past year and around 4% since the beginning of October.

To illustrate the chaos, we asked Claude to examine the 13F filings of the 25 largest dedicated healthcare hedge funds and identify their 25 most popular holdings.

We then asked Claude to chart the performance of these stocks this year.

The results show a 32.3% decline over the past month and a half.

Making matters worse, many healthcare funds also held significant short positions in stocks that surged dramatically, including $MRNA, $GRAL, $TWST, $IOVA, $NTRA, and others.

Naturally, this intensified the pain.

So, is the lesson to avoid popular stocks?

Not necessarily.

Even high-quality, attractively valued companies outside the market consensus have experienced aggressive selling.

It appears that investors have been selling quality stocks to chase speculative biotech names and large pharmaceutical companies.

One important lesson is that hedging through the $XBI ETF, which has substantial exposure to speculative biotech stocks, has provided relatively little protection against this particular market rotation.

What happens next?

One way to evaluate the opportunity is through forward valuations.

Using projected 2031 earnings, certain high-quality biotech companies appear to trade at significant discounts to the broader pharmaceutical industry.

An important distinction is that many of these companies have already successfully completed Phase 3 clinical trials or reached more advanced stages of development.

There are also numerous potential acquisition candidates, including:

$MDGL, $CELC, $COGT, $ABVX, $MLYS, $CGON, $BBIO, $MLTX, $PRAX, $PCVX, $BMRN, $CTMX, $GERN, $IONS, $NBIX, $CYTK, $TVTX, $SNDX, $SVRA.

Another attractive characteristic of some of these companies is that they may not need additional capital to reach profitability.

This distinction could become increasingly important if access to capital becomes more difficult.

The investment conclusion

Given these conditions, there appears to be little logic in selling high-quality, attractively valued mid-cap biotech companies simply to chase speculative stocks or large pharmaceutical companies trading at historically elevated multiples.

In fact, the current environment may offer an opportunity to establish or increase exposure to high-quality, mid-cap biotech value stocks.

“Anybody can go say, ‘AI is going to kill us,’ and you'll be on every major news station and every newspaper and so forth.

Ali Ghodsi from Databricks had a great formulation of, ‘Well, what would be the preconditions for that?’

And he had four preconditions.

One is that the next model has to require fewer GPUs than the last.

The second thing is the next model has to take less time to train.

And then the accuracy of the next model has to be better than the last, so it's got to be a better model.

And then finally, it's gotta keep happening again and again and again.

Zero of those four have been met.

We're not on track for any of those four to be met, and so we're really talking about a risk that's entirely theoretical at this point that we're not mapping to.”
